newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scientists surprised by Nobel awards.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scientists surprised by Nobel awards.

text.p: For Robert Richardson, the phone call telling him that he won the Nobel Prize for Physics on Wednesday was bittersweet.
"My first reaction was concern for my wife and daughter," he said. "It was a phone call at the same time of the morning that I found out my daughter was dead."

The Cornell University professor's eyes glistened as he recalled the pre-dawn phone call from Vanderbilt University in Tennessee nearly two years ago telling him his daughter Pamela, attending graduate school there, had died suddenly of heart failure.
His wife, Betty, is a physics lecturer at Cornell, in Ithaca, New York, and his other daughter, Jennifer, lives in Brooklyn, New York, where she plays violin in a rock band.

This time, the phone call was shocking in a different way. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced that Richardson, 59, won the 1996 Nobel Physics Prize along with two colleagues, David Lee of Cornell and Douglas Osheroff, now at Stanford University in Palo Alto, California.

They discovered the helium isotope helium-3 can be made superfluid at a temperature only about two thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Superfluidity is a scientific term for when a liquid is made so cold it loses all its usual molecular patterns.

A research team seeking to confirm the existence of cosmic strings -- immense objects thought to have been responsible for the creation of the universe -- was able to test its theories using the three men's discovery.
Lee, who held a news conference on the Cornell campus, said he was afraid he was dreaming when he got the early morning phone call from Sweden telling him he won the prize.

Osheroff said his first reaction was anger. "I said 'Do you realise its 2.30 in the morning?'," Osheroff told a news conference at Stanford University, where he is a physics professor. "I thought it was a family emergency until he said he was from Stockholm. That gave it away."
Describing the discovery of the superfluid helium-3, Richardson said in an interview in Washington, where he was attending a conference, "It's not something you are going to find in your kitchen."

It is, however, an important scientific tool. A California scientist is testing it to detect abrupt changes in the rotation of the earth. Another practical application involves magnetic resonance imaging, a technology used in medical diagnoses, Lee said.

Osheroff said his accidental scientific discovery when he was a graduate student showed what can be achieved when researchers "depart from the beaten path." He did an impromptu experiment with equipment the scientists were using for a different study when he saw "a kink" in the decrease in the rate of cooling of the helium-3 isotope.

At first he thought there might be something wrong with the apparatus, but he did the experiment again and saw the same thing. Lee and Richardson were his thesis advisers at the time and with Osheroff helped discover the first of three superfluid phases of liquid helium-3.

"It's very exciting. It's tremendously gratifying for me to see that the work I've done ... honoured by the Royal Academy," Osheroff, now 51, said in a telephone interview from his home. "Winning a Nobel Prize is a singular event. Next to that is being the first person in the world to understand something. That's what makes life exciting."
Osheroff said the discovery showed that "if you depart from the beaten path, there can be wonderful things out in the woods."
